subtype: Approach: anticipating questions with a friend [Action]
passage: Sahil booked the small meeting room in the hostel for Saturday evening. Madhav had agreed to play the tough examiner and had brought a list of questions written on the back of an old timetable. "Why this dataset and not a larger one?" "How do you know the result is not by chance?" "What would you do with more time?" Five in all. After each one, Sahil wrote an answer in a couple of lines. Two questions were easy. Two took a while to answer well. One, about the method's limits, could not be answered at all. Sahil marked it in red and put it on Sunday's reading list. They ended with tea, and Madhav gave a sober thumbs up.

qa.q: How many questions did Madhav ask?
qa.a: Madhav asked five questions in all.

qa.q: What was Sahil probably feeling when the question on the method's limits could not be answered?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt a bit uneasy but honest, since the question was marked in red and put on the reading list.

qa.q: What other approach could help Sahil practise, and why?
qa.a: Sahil could also answer the questions aloud to a phone recorder, because hearing the answers shows which sound unclear.

qa.q: How might Madhav see the role of tough examiner?
qa.a: Madhav is helping Sahil find weak spots early, and probably feels useful while doing it.

grounding: A listener acts as a tough examiner and asks five questions, and the student writes short answers and notes what needs more reading.
